author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This function counts letters that appear in **both lowercase and uppercase forms** within a word. It iterates through the word character by character, maintaining a `Set` of characters seen so far. For each character, it checks if the current character is in one case (lowercase or uppercase) and hasn't been seen yet, **but** the opposite case version **has** already been seen—if so, it increments the counter. This effectively identifies "special" letters that have at least one occurrence in each case, counting each such letter exactly once.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution uses an array of **52 elements** to track occurrences of each letter in both cases—positions 0–25 for lowercase and 26–51 for uppercase. It converts each character to its ASCII code and maps it to a position using `code - (code >= 97 ? 71 : 65)`. For each character, it checks if the current case version hasn't been counted yet (`arr[pos] === 0`) but the opposite case **has** been seen (`arr[(pos + 26) % 52] > 0`). When this condition is true, it increments the result counter, effectively counting each letter exactly once when it first appears in a different case than previously seen.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This is the **simplest and most direct approach**: it first converts the input word into a `Set` containing all unique characters, then loops through all 26 letters of the alphabet. For each letter, it checks if **both** the uppercase and lowercase versions exist in the Set using two `set.has()` calls. If both are present, it increments the counter. This method avoids the complexity of tracking character order by simply asking: "Does this letter appear in at least one uppercase and one lowercase form?"

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution is nearly identical to the second approach but uses an **`Int8Array`** instead of a regular `Array` for better memory efficiency. `Int8Array` is a **typed array** that stores only 8-bit signed integers, consuming less memory than a standard JavaScript array. Like the array-based solution, it maintains 52 positions (26 letters × 2 cases), maps each character to its position via ASCII code, and increments the counter when a character's case is seen for the first time while its opposite case has already been encountered.
